questions.q: What's the problem with a hard-coded list like WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IN (1, 2, 3)?
options: It always returns zero rows
It requires GROUP BY to work correctly
It's frozen at the moment it was written and can silently go stale as data changes
IN cannot accept a hard-coded list of numbers
questions.explain: If subcategories are added or removed, a hard-coded list no longer reflects reality.

questions.q: How many rows can a multi-value subquery used with IN return?
options: A maximum of 10 rows
Exactly one row, same as a scalar subquery
Exactly zero rows
Any number of rows — unlike a scalar subquery, which must return exactly one
questions.explain: IN is specifically built to handle a list of any size returned by the subquery.

questions.q: What is the advantage of using a subquery instead of a hard-coded list with IN?
options: Subqueries always run faster than hard-coded lists
There is no real advantage — they behave identically in every case
Subqueries can only be used with numeric values, unlike hard-coded lists
The list is generated dynamically, so it automatically stays correct as the underlying data changes
questions.explain: No hard-coded numbers to maintain — the inner query recalculates the matching set every time.

questions.q: What happens with NOT IN if the subquery's result set contains even one NULL?
options: NOT IN treats the NULL as if it were zero
The entire NOT IN comparison silently returns no rows, with no error
SQL Server raises an error immediately
The NULL is simply ignored and NOT IN works normally
questions.explain: This is a serious, silent gotcha — traces back to Lesson 16's NULL comparison behavior.

questions.q: What is the safer alternative to NOT IN when the subquery's results might contain NULL?
options: NOT EXISTS (covered fully in Lesson 55)
There is no safer alternative — NOT IN must always be used
NOT LIKE
NOT BETWEEN
questions.explain: NOT EXISTS avoids the NULL trap entirely, which is why it's generally preferred over NOT IN with subqueries.
